title: Distinct Integers That Cancel Out
statement:
Given n, return an array of n distinct integers whose sum is exactly 0.

Many arrays work; any valid one is accepted, in any order. Keep every value within ±1 000 000.

examples.why: Two mirrored pairs. [-5, 1, 2, 2] would also sum to 0, but the 2 repeats.
An odd count needs a middle value; 0 is the one that cancels itself.
A single number summing to 0 must be 0.

hints: What is the simplest way for two numbers to cancel each other?
Use pairs x and −x. They are distinct as long as x ≠ 0.
Add the pairs (1, −1), (2, −2), … for n / 2 rounds, and add a 0 when n is odd.

explain.intuition:
Any number and its negative cancel, so mirrored pairs ±1, ±2, … sum to 0 and never repeat. That covers an even n. For an odd n one slot is left, and the only value that cancels itself is 0, which no pair uses.

Another valid construction is 1, 2, …, n−1 followed by minus their sum. It is just as correct but produces a value around −n²/2, which is why the mirrored version is the usual answer.
pitfalls: Using 0 in an even-length answer and then running one value short or repeating one.
Looping pairs up to ⌈n/2⌉ for odd n, which returns n + 1 values.
Starting the pairs at 0, which puts 0 and −0 (the same value) in the array.

solutions.title: Count up, then balance
solutions.idea: Use 1 … n−1 and finish with minus their sum, which is always distinct because it is negative (or 0 when n = 1).

solutions.title: Mirrored pairs
solutions.idea: Pair each i with −i, and add 0 when n is odd.

followups: Return n distinct positive and negative integers summing to a given target t.
Return the lexicographically smallest valid array after sorting. What does it look like?
